title: Climate justice

definition.text: A form of environmental justice concerned with how unequally climate change harms marginalized and vulnerable people.

facts.text: It aims to share fairly both the burdens of climate change and the work of cutting emissions, through advocacy and policy change.
Those who gained most from industrialization, such as coal, oil and gas businesses, are seen as carrying most responsibility for the carbon dioxide built up in the atmosphere.
Many of the people and countries hit hardest by climate change did least to cause it.
When the people least responsible are also harmed by the responses to climate change, this is called the 'triple injustice' of climate change.
Views of climate justice fall into two groups: procedural justice, about fair and inclusive decision-making, and distributive justice, about who bears the costs.
Pakistan produces less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet its 2022 floods affected over 33 million people.
The richest 1% of people are responsible for twice as many emissions as the poorest 50%.
Lawsuits are one tool: a 2017 UN Environment Programme report counted 894 ongoing climate legal actions worldwide.

contested_note: The term is used in many ways, and its different meanings are sometimes disputed; whether capitalism itself is a root cause is also debated.

title: Burden-sharing principles in climate justice
article: Climate justice#Common principles of justice in burden-sharing

definition.text: Three rules for deciding who should carry the larger costs of climate change: those who caused most of it, those most able to pay, and those who benefited most.

facts.text: A 2023 study estimated the top 21 fossil fuel companies would owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative climate reparations over 2025–2050.
Some cities apply these ideas through intersectional adaptation policy; Barcelona requires 30% of new housing developments to be social housing.

definition.text: The fairness question raised because the generations mainly responsible for climate change are not the ones who will bear most of its damage.

facts.text: Under current pledges, children born in 2020 will face 2–7 times as many heat waves over their lives as people born in 1960.
Emissions from one generation can lock in damage for one or more future generations.
In April 2021 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court said one generation must not use up much of the CO2 budget and leave later generations a drastic reduction burden.

definition.text: Taking land and resources, often by foreign actors, in the name of environmental goals, in a way that produces unjust development; also called green colonialism.

facts.text: Land may be taken for ecotourism, protecting biodiversity or ecosystem services, carbon trading, or growing biofuels.
It is a narrower kind of land grabbing in which the motive is environmental, and it counts as a subtype of green imperialism.
Journalist John Vidal coined the term in 2008 in a Guardian article, 'The great green land grab'.
Carbon-trading firms may take land to plant trees and sell the resulting offsets.
The International Land Coalition says 59% of land grabs between 2000 and 2010 were for biofuels.
Green grabs cover thousands or millions of hectares and can drive Indigenous or peasant communities off their land.
Governments in debt are especially exposed, since they may sell public assets to avoid bankruptcy.
Critics worry the 30 by 30 protected-area target could bring new green grabbing.

title: Fortress conservation

definition.text: A conservation approach that tries to protect nature by creating protected areas cut off from people.

facts.text: The United States pioneered it; after the 1872 national park law, army cavalry guarded new parks, often expelling Native Americans.
Evicting residents to protect nature has been called the Yosemite model.
A UN special rapporteur says up to 250,000 people have been forcibly evicted for conservation projects since 1990; another estimate puts displacement between 10.8 million and 173 million.
Conservation charities have increasingly militarized anti-poaching work, sometimes arming paramilitary groups.
Ecotourism income and carbon credits from preserved forests are economic motives behind it.
Many Indigenous groups lack formal title deeds despite living in forests for centuries, which leaves them exposed to eviction.
Giving land title to communities has led to less forest clearing than state-run parks in the Brazilian Amazon, and community concessions in the Congo show less deforestation.
Evicted residents may end up working for extractive companies, so exclusion often leads to more exploitation of the land.

contested_note: Some conservation leaders argued for removing people from protected areas, while Indigenous rights advocates argue that handing land rights to inhabitants protects forests better.

title: Environmental defender

definition.text: A person or group that protects the environment from harms such as resource extraction, hazardous waste dumping, infrastructure projects or land seizure.

facts.text: In 2019 the UN Human Rights Council unanimously recognised their importance for environmental protection.
Global Witness counted 1,922 murders of environmental defenders in 57 countries between 2002 and 2019, about a third of them Indigenous people.
On average three defenders are killed every week, and up to one hundred are intimidated, arrested or harassed for every one killed.
The Environmental Justice Atlas documents over 3500 ecological distribution conflicts worldwide; Indigenous people are involved in 41% of cases.
Campaigns that succeed usually use many non-violent tactics; 26.7% of reported campaigns ended in the project being cancelled.
Many conflicts arise from renewable energy or conservation projects; hydroelectric dams are the most frequent cause in the renewable energy sector.
The 1998 Aarhus Convention gives individuals rights to environmental information, participation in decisions and access to justice.

contested_note: The term is disputed because it lumps together very different groups, many of whom do not call themselves environmental defenders or aim chiefly at protecting the environment.

title: Environmental justice

definition.text: A social movement against the harm done to poor or marginalized communities by hazardous waste, resource extraction and other land uses they do not benefit from.

facts.text: Hundreds of studies from the movement argue that exposure to environmental harm is unequally distributed.

The US Environmental Protection Agency defines it as fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people, regardless of race, colour, national origin or income, in environmental laws and policies.
The movement began in the United States in the 1980s, shaped by the civil rights movement and focused on environmental racism.
In 1982 residents of Warren County, North Carolina, protested a landfill for PCB chemicals; the six weeks of protest led to over 500 arrests.
A United Church of Christ study found race was the most important factor predicting where US hazardous waste facilities were placed.
Tighter waste rules in rich countries led to a surge of hazardous waste exports to the Global South in the 1980s and 1990s, which helped make the movement global.
It has added ideas such as ecological debt, environmental racism, climate justice, ecocide and sacrifice zones to political ecology.
It overlaps with movements for Indigenous land rights and for the human right to a healthy environment.

distinct_from: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South
notes: Sentence 22f23f520445 (History) repeats the claim that Indigenous territories hold about 80% of remaining biodiversity; Indigenous peoples page (1ec1cba70ff5) reports a 2024 Nature study finding that claim baseless, so it was left out.

title: Dimensions of environmental justice

definition.text: The main kinds of fairness environmental justice asks for: fair sharing of environmental benefits and burdens, a real say in decisions, and recognition of marginalized groups.

facts.text: Distributive justice means sharing benefits like clean water and green space, and burdens like pollution, equitably across communities.
Procedural justice means affected communities get information, take part in policymaking and have access to justice.
Recognition justice means respecting the distinct cultures and histories of marginalized groups, including Indigenous peoples.
Robert Bullard instead groups equity into procedural, geographic and social kinds; geographic equity concerns how close communities live to hazards such as landfills and incinerators.

distinct_from: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South

title: Critical environmental justice

definition.text: An approach created by David Pellow that questions the assumptions and gaps of earlier environmental justice studies.

facts.text: Its scholars hold that several forms of inequality together drive environmental injustice.
It rests on four pillars: intersectionality, spatial and temporal scale, seeking justice outside the state, and treating all beings as indispensable.

distinct_from: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South

title: Indigenous environmental justice

definition.text: Environmental justice as understood by Indigenous peoples, framed by their colonial situation and possibly aiming at decolonization.

facts.text: In the US, Native Americans fall under a separate legal regime as citizens of Indigenous nations, based on sovereignty recognised by treaty, not as ethnic minorities.
Scholars such as Dina Gilio-Whitaker argue that distributive justice assumes land is a commodity, which clashes with many Indigenous worldviews.

distinct_from: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South

title: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South

definition.text: The shifting of toxic waste from rich countries to the Global South, where weaker rules make disposal cheaper.

facts.text: Exports of toxic waste from the US escalated through the 1980s and 1990s.
Many receiving countries lack proper disposal systems, and local communities are not told about the hazards.
The Khian Sea incident, in which Philadelphia incinerator ash was dumped on a Haitian beach, contributed to the creation of the Basel Convention on international toxic waste movement.

title: Environmental racism

definition.text: The disproportionate burden of environmental hazards, pollution and ecological damage on marginalized communities and people of colour.

facts.text: It is built into policy-making at home and abroad and is a form of structural racism that creates health hierarchies.
Benjamin Chavis coined the term in 1982 while opposing a PCB waste landfill in Warren County, North Carolina.
Its causes include competition for cheap land, dismissive attitudes to harmful projects, and affected communities' lack of political power, mobility and money.
Some critics argue cost–benefit analysis can feed it by valuing environmental resources by their usefulness to society, through willingness to pay.
Communities of colour and low-income communities bear more of the air and water pollution from fossil fuel processing; such places are called sacrifice zones.
Between 1989 and 1994 an estimated 2,611 metric tons of hazardous waste went from OECD countries to non-OECD countries.
A US Government Accountability Office study after the 1982 Warren County protests was among the first to link the race and income of communities to hazardous waste sites.

notes: Sentence c1dac74286d6 carries a DUBIOUS flag; the fact is framed as a critics' claim.

definition.text: Payments or investments made to people judged to be harmed by the presence of industry.

facts.text: Possible recipients include people living near industry, disaster victims and climate refugees.
They can range from direct payouts to funds for cleaning waste sites, air monitors in low-income neighbourhoods, or public transport.

title: Traditional ecological knowledge

definition.text: Knowledge, practices and beliefs about how living things, including people, relate to each other and their surroundings, built up over generations and passed on through culture.

facts.text: It rests on long-term observation and experience rather than the standardized experiments of Western science, which has fuelled debate over how to use it in ecological management.
It is not a universal set of principles but a family of practices tied to particular places and worldviews.
It is usually kept as oral tradition, so it may lack the written records that legal claims require.
Its knowledge guides everyday needs such as weather reading, medicine, water management, farming, hunting, fishing and the classification of living things.
The 1987 UN report Our Common Future said Indigenous and tribal lifestyles could teach modern societies how to manage forest, mountain and dryland ecosystems.
Ecosystem management can combine science and TEK to gain long-term records that would otherwise be missing.
Climate change can make TEK less accurate, since Indigenous peoples rely on signs in nature to plan activities and forecast weather.
Whether Indigenous peoples hold intellectual property rights over their traditional knowledge is still debated in international law.

contested_note: Scholars debate how TEK should be combined with Western science and whether Indigenous peoples hold intellectual property rights over it; some critics call the term itself an appropriation.

title: Facets of traditional ecological knowledge
article: Traditional ecological knowledge#Aspects of traditional ecological knowledge

definition.text: Nicholas Houde's six-part breakdown of TEK: factual observations, management systems, past and current uses, ethics and values, culture and identity, and cosmology.

facts.text: Factual observations are long-term generalised observations, checked against accounts of other knowledge holders.
Management systems cover practices such as pest control, multiple cropping and ways of estimating the state of resources.
The ethics facet refers to environmental values that keep exploitation in check.

title: Indigenous cultural burning
article: Traditional ecological knowledge#Karuk and Yurok Burning

definition.text: Traditional controlled burning used by Indigenous peoples as a land management tool and spiritual practice.

facts.text: The Karuk and Yurok Tribes of California organised controlled burns in their ancestral lands to reduce wildfire risk and restore resources depleted by decades of fire exclusion.
An Indigenous nation in Australia that regained land reinstated its traditional controlled burning.
Colonists in California prohibited cultural burning in the late 1700s to early 1800s.

title: Access and Benefit Sharing Agreement

definition.text: An agreement that sets out how the benefits from using genetic resources are shared fairly and equitably.

facts.text: They usually arise from bioprospecting, where Indigenous knowledge guides the search for commercially valuable genetic and biochemical resources, and recognise that knowledge holders deserve a share.
Before the Convention on Biological Diversity, plant genetic resources were treated as common heritage of mankind and could be freely exchanged.
The CBD, in force from 1992, gave each state sovereign rights over genetic resources in its territory.
The Nagoya Protocol, adopted in 2010 and in force from 2014, requires access to take place with prior informed consent and on mutually agreed terms.
Monetary benefits include lump sums, milestone payments and royalties; non-monetary ones include shared research, joint intellectual property, technology transfer and training.

Digital sequence information can be used without physical samples, which escapes the access-based model; COP16 in Cali created a fund that gives half its resources to Indigenous peoples and local communities.
Biodiversity-rich developing countries push for stronger benefit-sharing duties, while developed countries with big users of genetic resources prefer narrower ones.
Under the CBD, parties should ease access to genetic resources for environmentally sound uses and share research results and commercial benefits fairly.

contested_note: The CBD's access and benefit-sharing principle provoked heated debate that left most stakeholders unsatisfied, and whether benefit-sharing should apply to freely available sequence data is disputed.

title: Free, prior and informed consent

definition.text: The principle that an Indigenous people must be consulted, bottom-up, before development starts on its ancestral land or uses resources in its territory.

facts.text: Free means no coercion or bribery; prior means consent is sought well before activities begin; informed means people get adequate information on the project's nature, size, pace and duration.
Critics note many treaties require only consultation, not consent, so Indigenous peoples cannot veto projects that affect them.
UNDRIP states that no relocation of Indigenous peoples may take place without their free, prior and informed consent.
The Philippines' Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 was the first national law to include it.
It has been applied widely in REDD+ forest projects; UN-REDD issued mandatory guidelines in 2013.
Industry representatives argue it lets Indigenous peoples block projects that could benefit the public; others reply that extraction for profit repeats neocolonial patterns.

contested_note: Definitions differ, and states and industry often treat it as consultation rather than a right to say no.

title: ILO Convention 169
article: Free, prior and informed consent#International Labour Organization

definition.text: An international treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples adopted by the International Labour Organization in 1989.

facts.text: It aims to end discrimination against Indigenous peoples and give them a role in decision-making, built on participation and consultation.
The duty to consult falls on the state, not on companies, and aims at agreement or consent to the proposed development.

title: Indigenous FPIC protocols
article: Free, prior and informed consent#Indigenous Peoples' FPIC protocols

definition.text: Rules written by Indigenous peoples themselves, since the early 2000s, for how consent processes must be carried out.

facts.text: The first protocols were sector-specific, the second were bio-cultural protocols tied to CBD access and benefit-sharing, and the third are autonomous protocols, mostly from Latin America.

title: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples

definition.text: A declaration adopted by the UN in 2007 that sets out the collective rights of Indigenous peoples, including self-determination.

facts.text: It covers rights to self-determination and to protect cultures, identities, languages, ceremonies and access to resources.
It does not define Indigenous peoples but affirms their right to decide their own identity.
It is the clearest statement of free, prior and informed consent in international development.
It offers benchmark standards on Indigenous land rights.

notes: No crawled page of its own; mentioned on many in-scope pages (Indigenous peoples, FPIC, Indigenous land rights, Ancestral domain, Harmony with nature, Sacred natural site).

title: Indigenous peoples

definition.text: Peoples marked by self-identification, cultural difference from others in their state, a special bond with their traditional territory, and a history of domination and discrimination; no single definition is generally accepted.

facts.text: There are some 5,000 distinct Indigenous peoples on every inhabited continent and in every inhabited climate zone.
Most are minorities in the state or territory where they live and have been dominated by other groups.
The UN has adopted no definition; its Permanent Forum holds that any single definition would be over- or under-inclusive.
Many states avoid the term and use labels such as 'scheduled tribes' in India or 'national minorities' in China.
Europeans justified colonising Indigenous lands partly by calling them terra nullius, 'no one's land'.
Since 2002 Indigenous environmental rights have gained international recognition, but few countries respect them in practice.

contested_note: There is no agreed definition, and whether particular African or Asian groups count as Indigenous is disputed.

conflicts.text: 21st-century estimates of the Indigenous population range from 250 million to 750 million.
conflicts.note: The lead (d157ee4d2687) gives 250 million to 600 million; a 2007 estimate (f206b4ad3db2) gave 750 million to a billion.

title: Indigenous land stewardship
article: Indigenous peoples#Environmental and economic benefits of the Indigenous stewardship of land

definition.text: The care of land by Indigenous peoples with secure tenure, which yields environmental and economic benefits for everyone.

facts.text: A WRI report says tenure-secure Indigenous lands generate billions, sometimes trillions, of dollars in benefits such as carbon storage, reduced pollution and clean water.
Such lands have low deforestation, cut greenhouse gas emissions, and limit erosion and flooding by anchoring soil.
At least 37% of remaining natural lands lie within Indigenous territories.
The often-cited claim that Indigenous peoples steward 80% of the world's biodiversity was found baseless by a 2024 study in Nature.

contested_note: The popular figure that Indigenous lands hold 80% of biodiversity is disputed; a 2024 study found it has no sound basis.
notes: Environmental justice page (22f23f520445) repeats the 80% claim as fact; verification should treat it as disputed.

definition.text: The disproportionate impact of climate change on Indigenous peoples worldwide compared with non-Indigenous peoples.

facts.text: There are over 370 million Indigenous people in more than 90 countries, and about 22% of the planet's land is Indigenous territory.
Some Indigenous scholars link these impacts to ongoing colonialism, seeing climate change as an intensification of settler colonialism's effects.
Indigenous farmers have long timed crops by wind direction, blooming, bird migration and other signs, which climate change disrupts.
Indigenous knowledge helps detect local climate impacts where scientific models often fail, and programmes shaped with Indigenous input have higher participation.
Indigenous people in the Ecuadorian Amazon were left out of the 2005 REDD+ project despite suffering deforestation's effects.
The Arctic is warming at twice the global rate, posing unprecedented challenges for its Indigenous nations.
Pacific islands have been lost to sea-level rise, displacing and killing Indigenous people.

definition.text: A conceptual and legal framework for studying and addressing how global warming affects international human rights.

facts.text: Governments, UN bodies, advocates and academics use it to guide climate policy under the UNFCCC and the core human rights treaties.
Most statements stress threats to the rights to life, food, water, health, housing, development and self-determination.
Human rights treaties rarely mention the environment; protection is derived from rights such as life, food, water and health.
In 2005 Inuit activist Sheila Watt-Cloutier petitioned the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights over US contributions to global warming; the petition was rejected but testimony was later heard.
The UN Human Rights Council unanimously adopted Resolution 7/23 recognising climate change as a threat to the full enjoyment of human rights.
On 8 October 2021 the Human Rights Council recognised a human right to a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment in resolution 48/13.
The UN Development Programme estimates an additional 600 million people will face malnutrition because of climate change.
Research suggests climate change may create some 50 to 200 million new displaced persons and refugees by 2100.

title: Climate refugees and human rights

definition.text: People forced to move by climate change who fall into a legal gap because such migration is not yet covered by international law.

facts.text: Climate-induced migration is one of the most disputed effects of climate change.
Asian and African mega-deltas and small islands face high flood and storm risk and large-scale displacement.
The International Organization for Migration defines environmental migrants as people obliged or choosing to leave home because environmental change harms their lives.

contested_note: How much migration climate change will cause, and who counts as a climate refugee, are disputed and undefined in law.

definition.text: The lands, territories and resources of Indigenous peoples, a term used especially in the Asia-Pacific region.

facts.text: Unlike land title, 'domain' covers spiritual and cultural ties to land, not just ownership that can be traded.
Indigenous peoples may prefer to be called custodians of their lands rather than owners; tradable private land was often introduced by colonialism.
The Philippines' Indigenous People's Rights Act of 1997 defines it to include lands, inland waters, coasts and natural resources held by Indigenous peoples or their ancestors.
The ILO's 1957 Convention No. 107 assumed Indigenous peoples would be integrated into wider society; it was replaced in 1989 by Convention No. 169.

definition.text: Taking the genetic resources and knowledge of farming and Indigenous communities without permission, to gain monopoly control through patents.

facts.text: Pat Mooney, founder of ETC Group, coined the term in the early 1990s.
A company patent can bar anyone, including the Indigenous group itself, from using or selling the resource.
Nearly one third of small-molecule drugs approved by the US FDA between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them.
Critics say the TRIPS agreement treats knowledge as private property and recognises inventions only if they can make industrial profit.
The 1992 CBD required host-country consent for bioprospecting and fair sharing of benefits; the 2010 Nagoya Protocol made this concrete.
The Nagoya rules had the unintended effect of blocking biodiversity research, as developing countries hesitated to approve even basic studies.
Critics label bioprospecting and biopiracy modern forms of extractivism.
The term was coined by Pat Mooney for profiting from indigenous knowledge of nature without permission or payment.

definition.text: A challenge to US and European patents on pesticide and antifungal products from the neem tree, used by Indian farmers for around 2,000 years.

facts.text: W.R. Grace patented a neem oil antifungal spray in 1994, although rural Indian farmers had used neem extracts for around 2,000 years.
The patent was overturned by the European Patent Office in 2000, and the neem tree became a symbol of resistance to corporate control of Indigenous knowledge.

title: Hoodia benefit-sharing case

definition.text: A dispute over a patented weight-loss compound from the Hoodia plant, long used by the San people, that ended in a benefit-sharing deal.

facts.text: South Africa's CSIR isolated the P57 molecule from Hoodia in 1996, and the patent rights were sold to Pfizer and Phytopharm.
After the San demanded restitution, a confidential agreement gave them royalties, knowledge exchange and jobs.

notes: 6efe48d70524 carries CITATION NEEDED; ea94d81cb56c flagged CONTESTED.

definition.text: The close link between climate change and poverty, since climate change hits poor people and developing countries hardest.

facts.text: Poor people face more exposure and vulnerability, meaning they are less able to cope with climate extremes.
The UN Development Programme says developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change.
A 2020 World Bank paper estimated climate change will push 32 million to 132 million more people into extreme poverty by 2030.
For poor households, a disaster, a bad harvest or an illness can be a crippling economic shock.
Climate-driven extremes could raise food prices by 3–84% by 2050.
Pro-poor adaptation links adaptation to poverty reduction; adaptation that ignores how poverty differs between people will be ineffective and unfair.
Poorer countries are hit harder yet have fewer assets and capacities to adapt.

definition.text: The idea that rich Global North countries have taken over most of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb greenhouse gases, leaving the Global South to bear the consequences.

facts.text: Global North countries, with 19% of world population, account for 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions; the Global South accounts for 8%.
Countries such as Ecuador emit relatively little carbon dioxide but have far fewer resources to cope with local climate impacts.

title: Climate apartheid
article: Climate change and poverty#Human rights and democracy

definition.text: A situation in which only the rich can escape the consequences of climate change.

facts.text: UN Special Rapporteur Philip Alston warned of it in June 2019, saying it could undermine human rights, democracy and the rule of law.
He cited Superstorm Sandy in 2012, when most of New York lost power while Goldman Sachs's headquarters had its own generator and sandbags.

definition.text: A conservation movement from the 1980s that involves local communities in protecting nature, in reaction to top-down conservation that ignored them.

facts.text: It grew out of opposition to fortress conservation, under which more than 20 million people are estimated to have been displaced.
In 1975 the IUCN first accepted that traditional ways of life could support biodiversity conservation.
The 2003 World Parks Congress and a 2004 CBD meeting recognised Indigenous peoples and local communities as governors of protected areas.
Co-management shares responsibility for protected areas between the state and local communities, blending traditional knowledge with science.
Livelihood strategies include ecotourism, rotational grazing, non-timber forest products, sustainable fisheries and carbon projects.
Community-managed lands in parts of Kenya have shown higher nutrient levels and plant productivity.
Benefits are often captured by local elites, while costs such as lost access to land fall on poorer households, as in Madagascar.
Legal recognition of communal land rights is essential for long-term success.

definition.text: A person, usually Indigenous, displaced from their homeland when a park or other protected area is created.

facts.text: Many were already marginalised, end up living on the edges of towns with few opportunities, and rarely have legal recourse against powerful conservation interests.
John Muir's view that wilderness should be cleared of inhabitants became US policy with the 1964 Wilderness Act.
In Guinea, 663,000 people have been displaced from protected areas; Liberia claims over 120,000 conservation refugees and Senegal has 65,000 displaced.
Anthropologist Darrell Posey argued that landscapes that look natural may be shaped by Indigenous peoples, who should be seen as models for conservation.

title: Ecocide

definition.text: The destruction of the environment by humans; the word joins Greek oikos, 'home', and Latin caedere, 'to kill'.

facts.text: An expert panel in 2021 defined it as unlawful or wanton acts committed knowing they are substantially likely to cause severe and widespread or long-term environmental damage.
Common causes include war, pollution, wanton overexploitation of resources and industrial disasters.
Olof Palme popularised the term at the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment, accusing the US of ecocide for using Agent Orange in Vietnam.
The US Air Force sprayed 20 million gallons of herbicides such as Agent Orange on 6 million acres of forests and crops.
The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court covers environmental damage only in wartime, not peacetime.
Ten countries have made ecocide a crime in peacetime, and campaigners seek to add it to the crimes tried by the International Criminal Court.
Destroying the environment can amount to cultural genocide by stopping people, especially Indigenous peoples, from following their way of life.

contested_note: Criminalising ecocide is proposed as a deterrent to corporations driving climate change, but others argue it would not address the crisis's root causes.

title: Ecological debt

definition.text: The debt some campaigners say the Global North owes the Global South for historical environmental injustice, such as resource exploitation, habitat damage and pollution.

facts.text: It has two main parts: ecological damage a country causes to others or to shared ecosystems, and its use of ecosystems at the expense of other countries' fair rights to them.
The term first appeared in 1985 in a booklet by German ecofeminist Eva Quistorp; Global South NGOs took it up in the 1990s.
Early reports took opposite approaches: a Chilean report treated it in moral and political terms, while a Swedish one tried to put a money value on it.
At the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, NGOs drafted a Debt Treaty demanding compensation for 500 years of damage; it was never recognised by international institutions.
At the 2009 Copenhagen talks, vulnerable countries demanded reparations for decades of excess pollution; the US envoy flatly rejected owing such a debt.
Climate debt, the best-developed attempt to quantify it, has two parts: adaptation debt and emissions debt.
Proposed ways to settle it include cancelling poor countries' financial debts or paying a basic income.

contested_note: How to define it, which past emissions count, and how it should be repaid are all debated, and some argue it risks commodifying nature.

definition.text: Attempts to put numbers on ecological debt, mostly by comparing each country's emissions with its fair per-person share.

facts.text: In 2000 Neumayer calculated a 'historical emissions debt': the gap between actual past emissions and equal per-capita emissions.
In principle a money value could be set by adding the external costs of past resource extraction to the share of global pollution poor countries bear from rich countries' consumption.
Matthews's 2015 method compares the warming caused by each country's emissions since 1960 with its population share of global warming.
A 'modified equal shares' approach weights each country's share of emissions by its basic needs.

title: Environmental conflict

definition.text: A social conflict caused by environmental damage or by unequal sharing of environmental resources; also called an ecological distribution conflict.

facts.text: The Environmental Justice Atlas documented 3,100 such conflicts worldwide as of April 2020, with many more undocumented.
They are rooted in the industrial economy: with less than 10% of materials and energy recycled, extraction keeps expanding at commodity frontiers.
A study of over 2743 conflicts found mining (21%), fossil energy (17%), biomass and land use (15%) and water management (14%) were the most challenged sectors; defenders were killed in 13% of cases.
Low-income countries see more conflicts over conservation, water and land; in high-income countries almost half concern waste, tourism, nuclear power and infrastructure.
Around 17% of conflicts in the EJAtlas record environmental justice 'successes', such as stopping an unsustainable project.
In environmental conflict resolution, the best predictor of success is adequate consultation with all parties.

notes: c46f46429100 carries CITATION NEEDED; the EJAtlas totals differ by date (3,100 in April 2020 in 79ef7eb4e42d; 3,500 by July 2021 in bd0b3fab9d60; over 3500 in 8bc4336af8e6).

title: Ecological distribution conflict

definition.text: A concept coined in 1995 by Joan Martínez-Alier and Martin O'Connor for conflicts over unfair access to natural resources and unequal pollution burdens.

facts.text: It extends the political-economy idea of economic distribution conflicts to unequal distribution of environmental resources.
Damage such as a factory polluting a river is often not valued by the market, so those harmed go uncompensated.
Neoclassical economics treats such impacts as externalities to price; ecological economists and political ecologists reject this monetary commensuration.
Movements may demand money compensation when weak (weak sustainability) but argue from values money cannot measure when strong (strong sustainability).

contested_note: Whether environmental harms can be priced and compensated, as neoclassical economics holds, is rejected by ecological economists and political ecologists.

title: Environmental gentrification

definition.text: A process in which cleaning up pollution or adding green amenities raises local property values and draws wealthier residents into a formerly polluted or neglected neighbourhood.

facts.text: Green amenities include parks, green roofs, gardens and green, energy-efficient building materials.
Greening can displace low-income households physically through rising housing costs, and can also displace long-time residents culturally, socially and politically.
The term was first coined by Sieg and colleagues in 2004 and combines the older topics of gentrification and environmental justice.
Green spaces tend to raise housing prices when housing supply is too small to meet local or regional demand.
Property prices near New York's High Line rose by 35%, and near Chicago's Bloomingdale Trail by 13.8% to 48.2%.
After Superfund cleanups, wealthier and more educated newcomers tend to move in while earlier residents are slowly priced out.
Cooling measures against the urban heat island, such as green walls and green roofs, can also trigger higher prices and displacement.

notes: The exact definition is called a topic of debate (909f41200566), but only as a hedge; not marked contested.

title: Environmental personhood

definition.text: A legal idea that gives certain natural entities, such as rivers or forests, the status of a legal person.

facts.text: Legal personhood gives the entity rights, protections, responsibilities and legal liability; because a river cannot go to court, a guardian acts on its behalf.
A legal person cannot be owned, so no one can own an entity that has been given legal personality.
Christopher D. Stone first proposed legal personality for natural objects in the 1970s in his article "Should trees have standing?"
New Zealand declared Te Urewera a legal entity in 2014 and the Whanganui River a legal person in 2017, represented by one guardian from the iwi and one from the Crown.
An Indian state High Court gave the Ganges and Yamuna legal-entity status in March 2017, but sceptics noted that the declaration alone would not stop their pollution.
In 2022 Spain recognised the Mar Menor lagoon and its basin as a legal person, the first ecosystem in Europe with its own rights.
Supporters say it lets people sue to protect nature without showing harm to humans, and honours Indigenous relationships with the land.
Critics note that a legal person can also be sued, raising questions about who is liable for harms such as natural disasters.

contested_note: The idea is controversial even among environmentalists, some of whom back rights of nature but not personhood as the way to secure them.

definition.text: Social movements that arise when poor people fight powerful state or private interests threatening their livelihood, health, sovereignty and culture.

facts.text: Unlike mainstream environmentalism, which centres on conservation and eco-efficiency, it puts social justice first.
Joan Martinez Alier describes it as the struggles poor people wage when they face ecological distribution conflicts, where an activity's environmental harms fall unevenly and unjustly.
Peruvian historian Alberto Flores Galindo suggested the term in 1988; in 1997 Martinez-Alier and Ramachandra Guha contrasted it with the 'full-belly environmentalism' of the global North.
Examples include the Chipko movement, Indigenous struggles against Brazilian agribusiness, and the Green Belt Movement led by Wangari Maathai.
Women often lead these movements because their daily roles, such as fetching water and growing crops, bring them into direct contact with nature.
Several leaders, such as Berta Cáceres and Chico Mendes, were assassinated for their activism.
Transnational environmental justice networks let local defenders seek international support against large corporations.

title: Varieties of environmentalism
article: Environmentalism of the poor#Varieties of environmentalism

definition.text: Martinez-Alier's division of environmentalism into three currents: the cult of the wilderness, the gospel of eco-efficiency, and environmental justice or the environmentalism of the poor.

facts.text: The cult of the wilderness, tied to the conservation movement, tries to separate economic activity from nature, mainly through reserves and protected areas.
The gospel of eco-efficiency accepts economic growth but seeks growth that uses fewer resources and makes less waste, the so-called dematerialization of the economy.
Critics of dematerialization say the entropy law limits efficiency gains, and that rich economies decouple only by outsourcing material-heavy production to poorer countries.
Wilderness thinking has at times expelled poor and Indigenous people from their lands to create reserves.

definition.text: The scientific study of how different groups of people understand the ecosystems around them and their relationships with their environments.

facts.text: Harold Conklin coined the term in his 1954 dissertation on how the Hanunoo culture relates to the plant world.
To learn how cultures classify their environment, ethnoecology borrows methods from linguistics and cultural anthropology.
It treats humans as part of ecosystems: people can act as a keystone species, shaping soil formation, seed dispersal and biodiversity.
According to the WHO, almost 80% of the world's population relies on ethnobotanical methods as a main source of treatment for illness.

title: Extractivism

definition.text: The removal of large amounts of natural resources, mainly for export, with little or no processing.

facts.text: The term was coined in Portuguese as "extractivismo" in 1996 to describe for-profit exploitation of Brazil's forest resources.
It is common across the Global South and the Arctic, but also occurs in sacrifice zones of the Global North.
Extraction has gone on for over 500 years; under colonialism, colonies in Africa, Asia and the Americas shipped resources to metropolitan centres.
Transnational corporations are the main actors, helped by weak governance in resource-dependent economies.
Resources such as gold, oil, lumber, water and food are taken by mining, drilling and deforestation, then processed elsewhere for world markets.
Extraction at this scale can turn renewable resources into non-renewable ones, because they are taken faster than nature can replace them.
Local and especially Indigenous communities often oppose it because it uproots them or degrades their quality of life.

notes: Some South American officials (e.g. Álvaro García Linera, 0af95f0ceddc) criticise the term itself, arguing all societies are extractivist to some degree (9bf80e411de6).

definition.text: A development model in which governments take greater control of resource extraction and its revenue in order to fund social programmes.

facts.text: It was adopted mainly by Latin American 'Pink Tide' governments during the commodity boom of the early 2000s.
States revise contracts, raise export taxes and push state ownership, while the economy remains export-driven.
Under Ecuador's Correa government, which expanded oil and mining, poverty fell by 37% and extreme poverty by 49%.
Critics say tying social programmes to commodity exports leaves them exposed to price drops and concentrates executive power.

definition.text: A feminist approach within political ecology that studies how gender shapes people's access to, control over and knowledge of natural resources.

facts.text: It argues that mainstream environmental policies rest on gender-neutral assumptions that can overlook women's knowledge of resource management.
It combines three areas it treats as gendered: knowledge, environmental rights, and grassroots activism.
It explains differences in environmental experience by social constructs of gender, not biology.
A key founding text is the 1996 book Feminist Political Ecology by Dianne Rocheleau and colleagues.

title: Green imperialism

definition.text: A critical label for what is seen as a Western strategy of influencing the internal affairs of developing nations in the name of environmentalism.

facts.text: Helge Ole Bergesen used it in 1988 to sum up how Third World elites viewed the Brundtland report.
The label eco-colonialism first appeared around debt-for-nature swaps from 1989.
Malaysia's leaders opposed European timber boycotts and palm-oil restrictions as imposing rich countries' priorities.
In 1994 Brazil, India and Singapore opposed linking trade to pollution controls, calling it hidden protectionism.

contested_note: The term is a derogatory epithet; a 1990s survey found 66% of respondents did not see debt-for-nature swaps as eco-colonialism.

definition.text: A principle of friendly, holistic coexistence between humanity and nature.

facts.text: It is used mainly in debates on sustainable development and the rights of nature.
The United Nations created a Harmony with Nature programme in 2009, and Bolivian support led to further General Assembly resolutions.
Bolivia's proposal for the 2012 Rio+20 conference argued that nature, like humans, has rights, including the right to exist and to regenerate its vital cycles.
The same proposal argued that GDP is an inadequate measure of well-being and called for indicators of environmental destruction.

definition.text: Territories and areas governed, managed and conserved in practice by Indigenous peoples or local communities, with clear benefits for biological and cultural diversity.

facts.text: Since about 2020 they are also called 'territories of life'.
An ICCA is marked by a strong bond between a community and a site, the community's leading role in managing it, and conservation outcomes even when conservation is not the aim.

The IUCN World Parks Congress of 2003 defined them as ecosystems with significant biodiversity voluntarily conserved by Indigenous and local communities through customary law or other effective means.
They may or may not meet the IUCN definition of a protected area, but when they do they can fit any IUCN category.
ICCAs are said to cover as much land as government protected areas, yet tens of thousands of sites lack government recognition.
Threats include mining, logging and other imposed development, and the takeover of community land to create state-run protected areas.
At CBD COP 10 in Nagoya in 2010, decision X/31 invited countries to recognise these areas and the communities behind them.

definition.text: The rights of Indigenous peoples, individually or collectively, to land and the natural resources on it, mostly in colonised countries.

facts.text: Land matters to Indigenous peoples for religious meaning, self-determination, identity and economic reasons.
In some Indigenous societies, earth and sea resources form the basis of the household economy, so ownership secures access to them.
Claims may rest on international law, treaties, common law, or national constitutions and laws.
Key international texts include ILO Convention 169 of 1989 and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples of 2007.
The gap between formally recognised land and land held and managed by custom is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental degradation.
In Brazil, only 14% of Indigenous lands ended up demarcated under 1983 laws, and much land was lost to mining companies.

definition.text: A common-law doctrine holding that Indigenous peoples' customary land rights survive after a settler state takes sovereignty.

facts.text: It is called native title in Australia, customary title in New Zealand and original Indian title in the US.
Indigenous land rights were long undermined by the doctrine of terra nullius, Latin for "land belonging to no one".
In Australia's Mabo case, begun by Meriam people in 1971, the High Court recognised native ownership and rejected terra nullius.
In the US case Johnson v. McIntosh (1823), the doctrine of discovery was used to rule that Native Americans had only occupancy rights to their land.

definition.text: The branch of law that deals with the rights to use land, transfer it, or keep others off it.

facts.text: In many places land is called real estate or real property, as distinct from personal property.
One person's encumbrance on land, such as an easement, may be another person's land right.
Land rights are so basic that they arise even without a state; the claim clubs of the American West enforced mining rules on their own.
Squatting, occupying land without owning it, happens all over the world.
Land reform means government policies that take or redistribute land, such as a land grant.
In customary-law places, customary land is the main form of ownership; in common-law places, Indigenous land rights are called aboriginal title.

definition.text: The ability to freely obtain, use and possess land, as long as doing so does not infringe on others' rights.

facts.text: Land rights differ from mere access to land: someone with only access can be expelled at the owner's choice, which limits financial stability.
Land law sets the legal rules on ownership, while land rights describe how far society accepts that ownership in practice.
UN research finds that rural landlessness strongly predicts poverty and hunger.
Customs often bar women from inheriting or buying land, leaving them dependent on male relatives even when they farm it.

definition.text: A facility or project, such as a landfill, power plant or prison, that a local community opposes because of the harms it expects from it.

facts.text: The expected costs include health hazards, ugliness, lower home values and sometimes higher utility costs.
Such facilities tend to end up in poor, minority or politically under-represented places that cannot fight them off.
Their harms keep high-earning buyers away, trapping low-income residents in a cycle of cheap housing near landfills and highways.
Of more than 1,000 US Superfund sites, 25% lie on or near Native American reservations.

definition.text: The idea of fairness in the processes used to settle disputes and share out resources.

facts.text: It concerns fair and transparent decision processes, in contrast with distributive justice (fair outcomes) and retributive justice (fair punishment).
Hearing all parties before deciding is one step that helps make a process procedurally fair.
Research by Tom R. Tyler found that simply giving people a voice, even one that does not change the decision, can be enough for a process to seem fair.
In 1976 Gerald Leventhal proposed six rules for judging procedures: consistency, bias suppression, accuracy, correctability, representativeness and ethicality.
Under the participation model, a fair procedure gives those affected a chance to take part in the decision.
In energy justice, procedural justice means access to information and meaningful participation in decisions.
In law it appears as due process in the US and natural justice in other common-law countries.

definition.text: John Rawls's division of procedural justice into perfect, imperfect and pure forms, set out in A Theory of Justice.

facts.text: Perfect procedural justice has an independent standard of a fair outcome and a procedure that guarantees reaching it.
Imperfect procedural justice has the independent standard but no procedure that guarantees the fair outcome.
Pure procedural justice has no standard of a just outcome other than the procedure itself.

title: Right to a healthy environment

definition.text: The human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, seen as necessary for enjoying rights such as life, health, food and water.

facts.text: The UN Human Rights Council recognised it on 18 October 2021 (HRC/RES/48/13), and the UN General Assembly did so on 28 July 2022.
The Human Rights Council vote was 43 in favour, none against and 4 abstentions; it was the first time the Council had recognised a human right in a resolution.
The General Assembly resolution passed with 161 votes in favour, none against and eight abstentions, though such resolutions are not legally binding.
165 countries recognise the right through their constitutions, laws or treaties they have ratified.
It protects the environment through its effects on individual people, unlike traditional regulation focused on other states or on nature itself.
It obliges states to regulate and enforce environmental law and control pollution, and has helped build legal precedent for climate change litigation.
The 1972 Stockholm Declaration recognised it in its first principle but was not legally binding.

notes: Also covers the page 'The human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment' (the UN resolution); one entry for both.

sources.title: The human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment

definition.text: The writing of the rights-of-nature theory into constitutions, statutes, treaties, local laws and court rulings.

facts.text: It treats ecosystems and species as having inherent rights, much like fundamental human rights.
As of 2022, nature's rights laws existed in 39 countries; initiatives numbered 409 in June 2021 and 495 in May 2024.
Ecuador's 2008 constitution gives nature, or Pachamama, the right to exist and regenerate its vital cycles, and lets any person demand those rights be respected.
In 2019 Bangladesh's High Court recognised the Turag River, and by extension all the country's rivers, as living entities with legal rights.

definition.text: A geographic area permanently damaged by heavy environmental change or economic neglect, often through locally unwanted land uses.

facts.text: A 2022 UN report found that millions of people live in pollution sacrifice zones, mostly around heavy industry and mining, and that marginalised groups are hit hardest.
Sacrifice zones go with 'abundance zones': damage in some places sustains privileges and lifestyles elsewhere.
A 1973 US National Academy of Sciences report on strip-mined coal lands in the American West introduced the term 'national sacrifice area'.
Louisiana's "Cancer Alley" is an 85-mile stretch along the Mississippi with over 200 petrochemical plants and a disproportionately black, low-income population.
Naomi Klein argued in 2014 that an economy run on fuels that release poisons when extracted and refined has always required sacrifice zones.

definition.text: The principle that people today should live and work for the benefit of the seventh generation to come.

facts.text: It is believed to come from the Great Law of the Haudenosaunee, which holds that decisions should be judged by their effect seven generations ahead.
The often-quoted line about considering the seventh generation does not appear in written transcriptions of the Haudenosaunee constitution, which instead urges leaders to consider future generations.
Some green economists advise measuring a project's impacts from the viewpoint of the seventh generation.

title: WIPO treaty on genetic resources and traditional knowledge
article: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge

definition.text: A 2024 international treaty, known as GRATK, that requires patent applicants to disclose when inventions are based on genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge.

facts.text: It aims indirectly to fight biopiracy and support access and benefit-sharing rules through its disclosure requirement.
It was concluded in Geneva on 24 May 2024 after more than two decades of work by WIPO's intergovernmental committee.
It is the first WIPO treaty with provisions specifically for Indigenous peoples and local communities.
It enters into force three months after 15 countries ratify or accede; 44 countries had signed by May 2025.

notes: Definition line of the dossier (f64bd5d577ae) is an image caption; definition built from 2d571c80ebd9 and eb9617e0c6aa.

sources.title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge

definition.text: The study of how political, economic and social factors relate to environmental issues and climate change.

facts.text: Unlike conventional ecology, it puts power relations at the centre of environmental issues.
It joins ecological social science with political economy, covering degradation and marginalisation, environmental conflict, conservation and control, and social movements.
A core assumption is that environmental change does not affect society evenly: political, social and economic differences shape who bears costs and who gains benefits.
Frank Thone first coined the English term in 1935; anthropologist Eric R. Wolf revived it in 1972.
Piers Blaikie's work on the social and political roots of soil erosion showed that problems blamed on local resource misuse often stem from the wider political and economic context.
It links today's uneven environmental burdens to policies and power relations rooted in colonialism.
Critics such as Vayda and Walters argue it presupposes the importance of political factors, and propose 'event ecology' instead.

title: Distributional effects of environmental policy

definition.text: How the costs and benefits of an environmental policy fall on different groups, and whether it widens or narrows environmental and social injustice.

facts.text: Distributional effects are one of the criteria, besides efficiency and cost-effectiveness, used to judge environmental policies.
A regressive tax is one whose rate falls as the taxed amount rises; a carbon tax that does not return its revenue is naturally regressive and hits the lowest incomes hardest.
A study found carbon pricing is on average progressive in countries with per capita incomes below USD 15,000 a year but tends to be regressive in richer countries.
Because carbon pricing is somewhat regressive, economists say poor people should be compensated.
A 2019 study found energy efficiency standards are more regressive than energy taxes.
Global estimates of climate damage costs usually leave out distributional effects.

contested_note: Whether carbon taxes are regressive is disputed; Gilbert Metcalf, for one, disputed that they would be in the US.
notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; facts drawn from Environmental policy, Carbon pricing in Canada, Climate change and cities, Regressive tax, Climate change in Turkey, Arik Levinson and Economic analysis of climate change. Contested note rests on e3d6322b8499.

title: Gender and environment

definition.text: The study of how relations between women, men and the environment shape resource use, the sharing of responsibilities and people's well-being.

facts.text: Interest grew from Ester Boserup's 1960s book Woman's Role in Economic Development; from the 1980s policymakers paid more attention to gender in resource management.
Women do 80% of food production in sub-Saharan Africa, 60% in Asia and 50% in Latin America, yet men generally own the land.
Improving women's access to farm resources could raise yields by 20–30% and total output in poor countries by 2.5–4%.
Feminist economists argue the growth paradigm keeps gender and environmental injustices in place and propose degrowth work-sharing.

notes: Phrase concept; the crawled page Women and the environment covers it, so it is used as the article.
